articles.title: BYD Claims 12-Minute EV Charging Even at -30°C
articles.description: BYD, the Chinese carmaker, has unveiled a new fast-charging system. The company says that it can charge an EV from 20% to 97% in 12 minutes despite the outside temperature as low as -30°C. It is powered by the second-generation BYD Blade Battery with Flash Charging tech. The company states that it takes the car about nine minutes to go from 10% to 97% in normal weather. It could reach a rate of 97% in 12 minutes in cold-weather testing, even at -30°C. EV charging normally slows down in the cold. When the weather is below freezing, batteries don't perform nearly as well. This has been a pain in the neck for electric car owners in colder locales for years. BYD claims to have solved the problem with its new system. Growing Charging Network BYD is also building more charging stations to support this technology. On August 28, the company opened its 10,000th Flash Charging station in China. These stations are now present in 332 cities across the country. BYD plans to expand further. The company wants to set up 20,000 Flash Charging stations across China by the end of 2026. This would make fast charging available to many more drivers. The system can deliver charging power of up to 1,500 kW. However, BYD notes that actual charging speed can change. It depends on the vehicle, battery size, charging equipment and weather conditions at the time. Also Read: Hyundai Ioniq 5 Beats Tesla in EV Battery Health Study What This Means? These numbers come from BYD itself. They have not been checked by an outside source yet. So the results may not be the same for every BYD vehicle or in every condition. Still, if these claims hold up in real-world use, they could be a big step forward for electric cars. Faster charging in cold weather would make EVs more practical in places with harsh winters. It could also ease one of the biggest concerns EV buyers have today. For now, drivers will have to wait and see if BYD's claims match real-life performance once more vehicles and stations are tested outside the company's own trials.
